method: An Albers map unrolls a cone that cuts the ellipsoid along two standard parallels, where the scale is exactly 1, and it is equal-area: the area of every region is the same on the map as on the ellipsoid, which is why it carries thematic maps of density, land cover and population rather than navigation charts. With the semi-major axis a, first eccentricity e and the functions m(phi) = cos phi / sqrt(1 - e^2 sin^2 phi) and q(phi) = (1 - e^2)[sin phi / (1 - e^2 sin^2 phi) - ln((1 - e sin phi)/(1 + e sin phi))/(2e)], the page computes the cone constant n = (m1^2 - m2^2)/(q2 - q1) for two parallels, or n = sin phi1 when both are equal (the single-parallel form), then C = m1^2 + n q1 and the radius rho = a sqrt(C - n q)/n. A point lands at x = rho sin(n dlambda) and y = rho0 - rho cos(n dlambda) east and north of the origin, where dlambda is the longitude from the central meridian wrapped into -180 to 180 degrees and rho0 is rho at the latitude of origin; the false easting and northing are then added, so the northing of the latitude of origin is the false northing. The scale along the parallel is k = rho n/(a m) and along the meridian h = 1/k, so k is exactly 1 on both standard parallels, the area scale h k is exactly 1 everywhere, and shapes stretch north to south between the parallels and east to west outside them. Grid convergence is n dlambda, positive east of the central meridian in a northern cone and negative there in a southern one, where the radius is negative and the inverse mirrors the (x, rho0 - y) pair before dividing the angle by n; that mirror is what keeps a southern grid point in its own quarter of the world. The defaults are the US national Albers grid (EPSG:5070) on GRS 80: 29.5 and 45.5 degrees north, origin 23 degrees north on 96 degrees west, which puts Washington DC at 1,618,883.3 m east and 1,924,594.2 m north with k = 0.990448. The inverse recovers q from rho, iterates latitude in up to 60 steps and reports longitude from theta/n; the page refuses a point on a pole, standard parallels on or across the equator, a latitude of origin in the opposite hemisphere, a latitude or longitude outside its range, and a grid position at or beyond the cone apex. Offered are WGS 84, GRS 80, Clarke 1866 and a mean-radius sphere; no datum shift, no false-origin azimuth, no grid rotation and no scale factor k0 are modelled, and the page does not draw the map. Pure local arithmetic: no upload, storage or network access.
